theme: The appointed offerings; the feasts; vows
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 28:1-30:16. These chapters give a calendar of offerings and the laws of vows. They may seem repetitive after the earlier readings in Leviticus, so read them with this question: why would God repeat this to a new generation?
settingTheScene: The first generation has died, and a new generation stands on the edge of the land. Moses restates the regular offerings and festivals to them. The daily offering, the Sabbath, the monthly new moon, and the annual feasts are all laid out, with their required sacrifices. Chapter 30 then deals with vows: who can make them, and who can annul them. The point is to prepare the people for life in the land, where worship will be part of daily rhythm.
observation: “Command the people of Israel and say to them, My food offering, my pleasing aroma, you shall be careful to offer to me at its appointed time” (28:2).
The daily offering is two lambs, one in the morning and one at twilight (28:3-8).
The Sabbath offering doubles the daily offering (28:9-10).
A monthly offering is made at the new moon (28:11-15).
Passover and Unleavened Bread are in the first month (28:16-25), the Feast of Weeks follows (28:26-31).
The seventh month has the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Booths (29:1-40).
“If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth” (30:2).
A father or husband may annul the vow of a daughter or wife under certain conditions (30:3-16).
interpretation:
The repeated calendar of offerings is for a new generation. The people who stood at Sinai are gone, and their children need to hear the law again. It is a lesson in how faith is passed on. Every generation must be taught. The things God has commanded do not become unimportant because they were said once.

The daily offering is the foundation of the schedule. Every morning and every evening, a lamb was offered. Everything else, the Sabbath, the new moons, the feasts, was added on top of this daily rhythm. The sense is that the whole of life is lived under the sign of sacrifice. At the beginning and end of each day, God is acknowledged and sin is covered.

The calendar also builds toward the seventh month. The feasts cluster there, the Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and Booths. The seventh month is the climax of the year, and it moves from the trumpet of awakening, through the cleansing of atonement, to the joy of the harvest. It is a movement that the church has always seen as a picture of the whole story of salvation.

The laws about vows come next. The principle in 30:2 is clear: a person must keep his word. Because a vow is made to the LORD, it is not something to be taken lightly. This is a hard word in an age when promises are cheap. The details about fathers and husbands annulling vows reflect the family structure of ancient Israel, and they show that vows were taken seriously enough to need regulation.

Behind all of it is the idea that worship is meant to be ordered. God does not leave it to our moods. He gives times, and he calls us to be faithful to them. This is not legalism. It is the discipline that keeps love alive.
connection: Jesus is the Lamb who was slain once for all, ending the need for daily sacrifices (Hebrews 10:11-14). Paul tells believers to “present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1), and Hebrews 13:15 calls for a continual sacrifice of praise. Jesus taught, “Let what you say be simply Yes or No” (Matthew 5:37), echoing the importance of keeping one’s word. Colossians 2:17 says that the festivals are “a shadow of the things to come.”
application:
Consider the daily rhythm of your own life. Do you begin and end the day with God?

Think about any promise you have made and not kept. Bring it to God and make it right.

Thank God that the daily sacrifice has been fulfilled in Christ, and offer him your praise today.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he is worthy of worship at every time.
Ask him to make you faithful to your word and to time with him.
Thank Jesus, the Lamb who took away your sin once for all.
